newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt weighs courting lone MP to boost coalition.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt weighs courting lone MP to boost coalition.

text.p: New Zealand's coalition government on Thursday showed signs it was considering a cabinet post for a solo legislator in a bid to shore up its voting power.
Earlier this week the centre-right coalition survived a threat to its current one-seat majority when a sacked junior minister pledged to continue supporting the government.
But parliamentary observers said Prime Minister Jim Bolger might offer a cabinet post to lone United Party MP Peter Dunne to bring his vote, and his party, into government.
Asked whether he would approach Dunne, Bolger said: "At the moment I am not ruling anybody in or out."
Dunne told Reuters earlier this week he was not prepared to be "the next substitute off the bench", and expected a lengthy negotiating process before any deal was struck.

The capital's Dominion newspaper, seen as sympathetic to the government, said in an editorial on Thursday that criticisms of Bolger by sacked associate health minister Neil Kirton, even after he had pledged his vote to the coalition, underlined the need to bring Dunne into the executive.
"That makes it clear that relying on Mr Kirton to provide the voting muscle the government needs to guarantee the progress of its legislation is foolish," the article said.
It added Kirton could continue to threaten paralysis of the legislative process. "The antidote to that is obvious: include ... Dunne in the executive as soon as possible."
But political commentator Colin James said he did not expect Bolger to rush into a decision. "If there ain't a fire don't put it out," James said.

"(Dunne) would want a cabinet post and some changes to the coalition agreement. My assessment is that Bolger will be in no hurry to do that because he hasn't got an immediate crisis on his hands. He has the alternative option of toughing it out as a minority government," James added.
The coalition agreement between Bolger's conservative National Party and the smaller nationalist New Zealand First Party struck in December allows other parties to join.
Dunne was Revenue and Internal Affairs Minister in the previous National-led government and was a Labour MP before leaving and later joining United.
While his party calls itself centrist, Dunne is seen as fiscally dry and has argued against postponing tax cuts.
National Party strategists are keen to take the heat out of any future internal problems and neutralise the potential for any one MP to erase the government's majority.

As it stands, a single defection from the 61-vote block formed by NZ First and National in the 120-seat house would not threaten the government's survival or its economic programme because Dunne and eight free-market Act Party MPs have pledged their backing on confidence and core fiscal issues.
But the loss of an absolute majority would hamper the government's control of parliament and undermine confidence.
The government is already weakened by a series of minor scandals involving individual MPs.
In a TV1 poll released on Wednesday the disapproval rating of the government's performance was 77 percent, with approval just 14 percent.
